notes: PRI moved from MD slot 2 to ruling slot 0 (pro-Western autocrats). Coalition slot 13 holds the Ortiz Mena / Banco de México technocracy that runs the economy for the PRI presidency. CTM placed in 3 as the ORIT-affiliated labour pillar; PPS in 19 as national-communist satellite; PARM in 20. Slots 8-12 are small immigrant/student circles (no organised Islam in 1970 Mexico).

0.name: Partido Revolucionario Institucional
0.text:
Heir of the Partido Nacional Revolucionario founded by Plutarco Elías Calles in 1929, the PRI has not lost a presidential, gubernatorial or Senate race in four decades. President Gustavo Díaz Ordaz governs under the shadow of the October 1968 massacre at Tlatelolco, while party president Alfonso Martínez Domínguez steers the campaign of Luis Echeverría, unveiled as the next presidential candidate in November 1969.

The party is less an ideology than a state machine: its labour, peasant and popular sectors bind the CTM, the CNC and the bureaucracy to the presidency, and every six years the outgoing president anoints his heir. It keeps Washington close through trade and quiet anticommunism, yet guards a nationalist foreign policy that still recognises Castro's Cuba.

1.name: Partido Acción Nacional
1.text:
Founded in 1939 by Manuel Gómez Morín as the voice of Catholic professionals and businessmen repelled by Cardenismo, Acción Nacional is Mexico's only opposition party of any weight. Under president Manuel González Hinojosa it is preparing to run Efraín González Morfín, son of co-founder Efraín González Luna, against Echeverría in July 1970, after the regime annulled its 1968 municipal victories in Tijuana and Mexicali.

The PAN preaches clean elections, municipal freedom, private property and the social doctrine of the Church, with González Morfín pushing a more solidarist, reform-minded line. Its strongholds are Mérida, the northern border cities and the Catholic middle classes of Guadalajara and Puebla. It is firmly anticommunist and Western in outlook, but its real weapon is moral: it denounces fraud the PRI cannot hide.

2.name: Liberales Reformadores Juaristas
2.text:
Inside the revolutionary family a loose network of lawyers, intellectuals and senior officials invokes Benito Juárez and the liberal Reform to argue that the system must open up after Tlatelolco. Its most respected figure is Jesús Reyes Heroles, director of Pemex and historian of Mexican liberalism; many of its members once rallied to Carlos A. Madrazo, the PRI president ousted in 1965 for proposing open party primaries, who died in a plane crash in June 1969.

The reformers want honest vote counts, a larger role for opposition deputies, a freer press and a party that chooses candidates from below. They defend the secular state, the mixed economy and Mexico's independent diplomacy. Their leverage lies in their access to the cabinet and in Echeverría's need to win back students and intellectuals.

3.name: Confederación de Trabajadores de México
3.text:
Founded in 1936 under Vicente Lombardo Toledano, the CTM became the labour pillar of the ruling party once Lombardo was pushed out in the late 1940s. Since 1950 it has been run without interruption by Fidel Velázquez, the patient boss who placed loyal 'charro' leaders over the unions, and it anchors the Congreso del Trabajo created in 1966 to bring the country's federations under one roof.

The CTM trades industrial peace for wage gains, social security, housing and seats on PRI electoral lists, and it has won a new Federal Labour Law that takes effect in 1970. Affiliated with the US-backed ORIT, it is resolutely anticommunist and applauded the crushing of the 1959 railway strike. Its strength is numbers: hundreds of thousands of members and a veto over strikes.

4.name: Partido Comunista Mexicano
4.text:
Founded in 1919, the Mexican Communist Party has no legal registration and lives between tolerance and repression. Its general secretary Arnoldo Martínez Verdugo leads a party battered by the crackdown on the 1968 student movement: militants and sympathisers fill the cells of Lecumberri prison alongside the railway leader Demetrio Vallejo, jailed since 1959.

The PCM calls for democratic liberties, independent unions, agrarian reform and the release of political prisoners, and seeks a broad democratic front rather than armed struggle. It belongs to the Soviet-aligned movement but condemned the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia, a sign of growing autonomy. Its base lies among university students, teachers, railwaymen and intellectuals, and its influence in the universities far exceeds its few thousand members.

5.name: Partido de los Pobres
5.text:
The Party of the Poor was born in the Sierra de Atoyac in Guerrero in 1967, when the rural schoolteacher Lucio Cabañas took up arms after police fired on a parents' protest in Atoyac de Álvarez. Its armed wing, the Brigada Campesina de Ajusticiamiento, moves among the coffee and copra smallholders of the Costa Grande, while Genaro Vázquez's rival Asociación Cívica Nacional Revolucionaria operates in the same state.

Cabañas preaches a peasant revolution against caciques, logging companies, coffee middlemen and the PRI state, drawing on Marxism, Zapatista memory and Christian notions of justice. He rejects both the PCM's legal road and Moscow's discipline. His leverage is the mountains themselves, the loyalty of poor villages and the regime's fear that the radicalised students of 1968 will join the guerrilla.

6.name: Movimiento Universitario de Renovadora Orientación
6.text:
MURO appeared at the National University in the early 1960s as the public face of El Yunque, a secret Catholic society founded in Puebla in 1953 to fight communism, freemasonry and the liberal state. Its shock groups clashed with leftist students throughout the decade and denounced professors as Marxist agents, while sister cells work in Puebla, Guadalajara and the Bajío.

The movement dreams of a Catholic, Hispanic and corporatist Mexico in the spirit of the Cristeros. It despises the PRI's secular revolution, but also Protestant missions, American mass culture and liberal democracy as corrupting imports. It recruits idealistic students from Catholic schools and enjoys discreet backing from conservative businessmen and clergy; its leverage lies in quietly infiltrating Catholic associations and the PAN.

7.name: Dirección Federal de Seguridad
7.text:
Created in 1947 under President Miguel Alemán and now attached to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Security Directorate is the regime's political police. Fernando Gutiérrez Barrios, a former army officer, has directed it since 1964; his agents infiltrated the 1968 strike committees, coordinated arrests after Tlatelolco and now hunt the guerrillas of Guerrero and the urban cells forming among radical students.

The DFS watches parties, unions, journalists and foreign embassies, and keeps files on the regime's own politicians. It swaps information with the CIA station in Mexico City, yet answers only to the president and the Interior Secretary. It favours a closed, policed order in which dissent is bought or broken; its leverage is knowledge, fear and the power to fabricate a scandal.

8.name: Hermandad Amilí de México
8.text:
A small benevolent association of Shia families from Jabal Amil in southern Lebanon, the Amili Brotherhood lives in the shadow of the far larger and mostly Maronite Lebanese colony of La Merced, Puebla and Mérida. It has no mosque; its members gather in private homes for Muharram mourning and send money to relatives around Nabatieh and Tyre.

The brotherhood follows with pride the rise of Imam Musa al-Sadr, whose Supreme Islamic Shia Council opened in Beirut in 1969 to claim a fairer share for Lebanon's Shia. It preaches a moderate, civic Shiism: education, communal charity, good relations with Christians and loyalty to Mexico. Its leverage is modest, resting on trade networks and the goodwill of successful Lebanese-Mexican businessmen.

9.name: Círculo de Nayaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a handful of young Shia men, sons of Lebanese immigrants and a few foreign students, who meet in Mexico City to read lectures smuggled from the seminaries of Najaf. There Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini has lived in exile since 1965, and the Iraqi cleric Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr is turning Shia learning into a political doctrine.

The circle rejects the quietism of its elders and argues that religious scholars must guide public life. It loathes the Shah of Iran, Israel and the American power that sustains both, and regards Mexico's secular revolution with suspicion. It has no institutions, funds or public face; its only leverage is the fervour of its members and the contacts they keep with militant clerical networks in Iraq and Lebanon.

10.name: Comité Pro-Mezquita de México
10.text:
The Mosque Committee gathers Sunni merchants of Palestinian, Syrian and Lebanese origin, joined by Arab diplomats posted to Mexico City, around one goal: building the capital's first proper mosque. Until then Friday prayers rotate between offices and private homes, and the committee seeks patrons among the Gulf monarchies and the Muslim World League founded in Mecca in 1962.

Its religion is conservative, obedient and apolitical: respect for rulers, correct ritual, Arabic and Koran classes for children, and literature printed in Saudi Arabia. It avoids any clash with Mexico's anticlerical laws and keeps cordial ties with the Interior Ministry. Its leverage is money and patience; should Saudi or Kuwaiti funds arrive, it would become the official face of Islam in Mexico.

11.name: Estudiantes del Tahrir
11.text:
A tiny cell of Jordanian and Palestinian students at the National University and the Polytechnic, the Students of the Tahrir circulate the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani. They meet discreetly, wary of both the Mexican police and the Jordanian embassy.

Their goal is the restoration of a single caliphate uniting all Muslims under Islamic law, which they see as the only answer to the defeat of 1967. They reject nationalism, elections, communism and capitalism alike, and regard every existing Arab state as illegitimate. Outside a few student rooms they have no audience, but they debate fiercely with the Palestinian leftists who dominate Arab student life abroad.

12.name: Asociación Islámica de México
12.text:
The Islamic Association gathers Egyptian and Syrian professionals, Arab students and a handful of Mexican converts in rented rooms in Colonia Roma, where they hold Friday prayers, Arabic lessons and lectures. Several members admire the Muslim Brotherhood, crushed by Nasser in 1954 and again in 1965, and read Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb, hanged in Cairo in 1966.

The association calls for an Islamic renewal that is neither capitalist nor communist, and for solidarity with Palestine after the Six-Day War. It seeks converts through education and charity rather than confrontation and respects Mexico's laws. Its leverage is intellectual: books from Cairo and Geneva, contacts with Said Ramadan's Islamic Centre, and an ability to speak to curious Mexican students.

13.name: Tecnocracia del Desarrollo Estabilizador
13.text:
Mexico's economic miracle has two faces: Antonio Ortiz Mena, Finance Secretary since 1958, and Rodrigo Gómez, director of the Bank of Mexico since 1952. Around them stands a corps of economists from Hacienda, the central bank and Nacional Financiera who have kept the peso fixed at 12.50 to the dollar since 1954, held inflation low and delivered growth of over six per cent a year.

The technocrats serve the PRI presidency but see politics as an obstacle to sound management. They favour import substitution, cautious public spending, foreign credit and an alliance with private industry, and they distrust both populist spending and the campaign rhetoric of Echeverría. Their leverage is the budget, the banks and the confidence of foreign lenders, which no president dares lose.

14.name: Acción Católica Mexicana
14.text:
Founded in 1929, the year the bishops made peace with the state and ended the Cristero War, Mexican Catholic Action organises men, women and youth under the direction of the hierarchy. Under the watch of Cardinal Miguel Darío Miranda, Archbishop of Mexico, it works within a Church barred by the 1917 Constitution from politics, property and worship outside its temples, yet it fills the country's churches every Sunday.

Catholic Action works through schools, parishes, parents' unions and charities, demanding religious freedom in education and defending family and morality against secular schooling and the official free textbook. Since Vatican II and the Medellín conference of 1968 it is torn between conservatives and progressives like Bishop Sergio Méndez Arceo of Cuernavaca. Its leverage is the faith of millions.

15.name: Grupo Monterrey
15.text:
The Monterrey Group is the informal alliance of the Garza Sada and allied families who built the Cervecería Cuauhtémoc, the Hylsa steel works, the Vidriera glass company and the Monterrey Institute of Technology. Its patriarch Eugenio Garza Sada is the most respected industrialist in the country and the symbol of a northern bourgeoisie that owes little to the capital.

The group believes in private enterprise, paternalist company welfare, technical education and Catholic values. It distrusts the PRI's populism, state companies and the official unions, and funds its own white unions to keep the CTM out. Firmly pro-American and anticommunist, it negotiates with presidents as an equal; its leverage is investment, employment in Nuevo León and the threat of capital flight.

16.name: Confederación Patronal de la República Mexicana
16.english: Employers' Confederation of the Mexican Republic
16.native_full: Confederación Patronal de la República Mexicana
16.text:
COPARMEX was founded in Monterrey in 1929 by Luis G. Sada and other northern industrialists to resist the planned federal labour code, and it has remained the voluntary, militant voice of private employers ever since. Unlike the chambers of commerce and industry, membership is not compulsory, which makes it the most outspoken business body in the country.

The confederation preaches free markets, limited government, the sanctity of private property and the freedom to hire and fire. It fought the new Federal Labour Law that takes effect in 1970 and attacks state companies, price controls and union privileges as steps toward socialism. Its members are mostly medium-sized firms of the north and the Bajío, and its leverage lies in lobbying, press campaigns and links with the PAN.

17.name: Instituto Mexicano de Recursos Naturales Renovables
17.english: Mexican Institute of Renewable Natural Resources
17.native_full: Instituto Mexicano de Recursos Naturales Renovables
17.text:
Founded in 1952 by the biologist Enrique Beltrán, the Mexican Institute of Renewable Natural Resources is the country's pioneering conservation body and heir to the forest crusade of Miguel Ángel de Quevedo. Beltrán, undersecretary for forests under López Mateos, uses the institute to publish studies, train foresters and lobby ministers on soil erosion, deforestation and wildlife.

The institute argues that Mexico's growth is consuming its forests, waters and soils, and calls for rational resource management, national parks and education rather than confrontation. It is apolitical and technocratic, working with universities, the FAO and American conservation groups. Its audience is small, but its warnings about the drying lakes of the Valley of Mexico and the logging of the Sierra Madre find echoes among scientists and officials.

18.name: Sindicato de Trabajadores Electricistas de la República Mexicana
18.english: Union of Electrical Workers of the Mexican Republic
18.native_full: Sindicato de Trabajadores Electricistas de la República Mexicana
18.text:
The electricians' union of the power industry nationalised in 1960 is led by Rafael Galván, a veteran organiser who keeps alive the left-nationalist spirit of Lázaro Cárdenas inside the official labour world. Galván's union stands apart from Fidel Velázquez's CTM and jealously defends its own elections, assemblies and contracts against rival unions favoured by the government.

The STERM argues that the Mexican Revolution has been betrayed by bosses, bankers and union bureaucrats, and calls for union democracy, a stronger state sector, economic planning and renewed agrarian reform. It looks to the Third World rather than to either bloc. Its leverage lies in the national power grid, alliances with independent peasants and teachers, and its ability to shame the regime with its own revolutionary language.

19.name: Partido Popular Socialista
19.text:
Founded in 1948 by Vicente Lombardo Toledano as the Partido Popular and renamed in 1960, the PPS lost its founder in November 1968 and is now led by general secretary Jorge Cruickshank García. It is a registered party with a few party deputies, and it will again endorse the PRI's presidential candidate, as it has done since 1958.

The PPS calls itself Marxist-Leninist but holds that the Mexican Revolution must be pushed forward from within, through nationalisations, state planning, agrarian reform and an anti-imperialist foreign policy. It admires the Soviet Union and Cuba but rejects confrontation with the regime, denouncing the guerrillas as adventurers. Its base is shrinking: teachers, some peasant leagues and old Lombardista unionists; its leverage is its legal registration and its place in the system.

20.name: Partido Auténtico de la Revolución Mexicana
20.english: Authentic Party of the Mexican Revolution
20.native_full: Partido Auténtico de la Revolución Mexicana
20.text:
The PARM was founded in 1954 by veteran generals of the Revolution, among them Jacinto B. Treviño and Juan Barragán, to defend what they call the authentic principles of 1910 against the careerists of the new PRI. Barragán, once chief of staff to Venustiano Carranza, presides over the party, whose registration survives with the government's blessing.

The PARM offers patriotic nationalism, respect for the army, order, property and the Constitution of 1917, and dislikes both communists and Catholic politicians. It always endorses the official presidential candidate and will back Echeverría in 1970. Its supporters are veterans, small-town notables and businessmen of Tamaulipas and the northeast; its leverage is a handful of party deputies and its usefulness as a loyal pseudo-opposition.
20.wiki: Authentic Party of the Mexican Revolution

21.name: Unión Nacional Sinarquista
21.text:
Founded in León, Guanajuato in 1937 by Catholic militants, many of them heirs of the Cristero struggle, the National Synarchist Union once marched hundreds of thousands of peasants in disciplined columns and openly admired Franco's Spain. Its party was banned in 1949 and quarrels have split it, but it survives as a smaller, tenacious movement of the Bajío, Michoacán and the Jalisco highlands.

Synarchism rejects both liberal democracy and communism, and dreams of a Christian social order of families, municipalities and corporations under a strong authority. It is Hispanist, anti-Yankee, anti-Masonic and hostile to the revolutionary state's secularism. Its base is poor Catholic smallholders and migrants to the United States; its leverage is the discipline of its cadres and its plans for a new electoral vehicle.

22.name: Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional
22.text:
Mexico's army has not produced a president since Manuel Ávila Camacho left office in 1946, and the generals have accepted a loyal, apolitical role in exchange for budgets, promotions and discreet business opportunities. Defence Secretary General Marcelino García Barragán commands an army organised in military zones that double as instruments of regional control.

In 1968 the army occupied the National University and fired on the crowd at Tlatelolco, and it now runs counterinsurgency sweeps in the mountains of Guerrero. The officer corps is nationalist, anticommunist and wary of American tutelage, accepting only modest US aid. Its leverage lies in being the regime's final guarantee: no president can survive without the army's loyalty, and the generals know it.

23.name: Casa Imperial de Iturbide
23.text:
Mexico has twice been an empire: under Agustín de Iturbide in 1822-1823 and under Maximilian of Habsburg from 1864 until his execution at Querétaro in 1867. The childless Maximilian adopted two of Iturbide's grandsons as heirs, and the dynastic claim has since passed to descendants of the Iturbide family living in Europe, far removed from Mexican politics.

Monarchism survives as nostalgia among a few conservative Catholic families, Hispanist scholars and admirers of Maximilian and Carlota, who see the Second Empire as a lost chance for order, faith and civilisation. They have no organisation of weight and no hope under the revolutionary state. Their only leverage is symbolic: history, the cult of the liberator Iturbide and the romance of the Habsburg court at Chapultepec.
